newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa may face 700,000 T yellow maize shortfall.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa may face 700,000 T yellow maize shortfall.

text.p: South Africa faces a yellow maize shortage of up to 700,000 tonnes this season and may have to import maize from the U.S., despite a bumper local harvest.

Domestic supplies have been drained by a high level of exports, large-scale deliveries to the export pools of the state-owned Maize Board and a slightly lower-than-expected crop yield, industry observers said on Wednesday.
Kit Le Clus, research and development manager at the National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo), said the national shortage could be as high as 691,000 tonnes.
The actual shortfall may be less if some maize earmarked for export finds its way back onto the domestic market.

According to Le Clus, South Africa has 4.478 million tonnes of yellow maize in the 1996/97 season, comprising new production and carryover stocks. Demand, which includes commercial use, private exports, Maize Board pool deliveries and end stocks amounted to 5.169 million tonnes.
The shortage appears to be most acute in coastal areas, which are furthest from the central maize growing belt. The Western Cape province alone is expecting a shortfall of about 200,000 tonnes.

"We would need until the end of the season (end-April 1997) in the vicinity of 200,000 tonnes...only in the Western Cape," said Francois van der Merwe, chairman of the Western Cape Maize Buyers Association.
The association last month opened a tender to import maize, and recently raised the amount to 170,000 tonnes from 70,000 before, van der Merwe told Reuters.
He said yellow maize, which is used for animal feed, would be imported from the U.S. "The U.S. tends to be the only source."
Nampo's Le Clus, however, cautioned that deficit projections were "theoretical" and that there could in reality be "a lot of maize around".

The Maize Board on Wednesday told Reuters it had maize stocks available in its export pools, but declined to disclose the amount. Farming co-operatives are also believed to be hanging onto stocks in the hope of securing higher prices.

Giep Steenkamp, the Maize Board's director of international marketing, said the Board might sell maize back onto the domestic market but would have to comply with this season's marketing scheme, which states such sales be priced at import parity plus 20 rand a tonne.
He said import parity on yellow maize at port of entry last Friday was about 793 rand a tonne.

"So if the people are willing to pay the importy parity, it is possible (we may sell maize domestically)...With world prices coming down there is a possibility that the local market can afford it, especially in the coastal areas," Steenkamp said.
South Africa is expected to have a surplus of white maize this season based on an estimated crop of 5.44 million tonnes.
